entities.name: The work is motivated by unresolved structural identification issues in orthorhombic samples—specifically the unclear origin of the 47° peak in the low-TO ortho
entities.description: The work is motivated by unresolved structural identification issues in orthorhombic samples—specifically the unclear origin of the 47° peak in the low-TO orthorhombic sample, which may come from residual tetragonal material—and therefore by the need for systematic studies to test whether orthorhombic-superstructure signatures can be detected and analyzed using simpler, more accessible techniques.
entities.evidence_span: From what has been said above, it is unclear whether the peak at 47o characteristic of the Tetragonal phase and observed only in the Orthorhombic phase obtained at low TO, arises from residual material still in the Tetragonal phase.

evidence_spans: From what has been said above, it is unclear whether the peak at 47o characteristic of the Tetragonal phase and observed only in the Orthorhombic phase obtained at low TO, arises from residual material still in the Tetragonal phase.

This, in turn, motivates the need for systematic studies aimed at determining whether structural signatures associated with the dif-ferent Orthorhombic superstructures can be detected and analyzed using simpler and more accessible experimental techniques, such as conventional X-Ray diffrac-tion, magnetic and electric measurements, and even complementary structural- and electronic-sensitive methods.

entities.description: Prior work on YBCO superstructures has primarily relied on bulk-sensitive probes—especially synchrotron high-energy X-ray diffraction and neutron scattering—to directly study oxygen ordering in the bulk; neutron diffraction further showed that different orthorhombic superstructures have distinct oxygen occupancies (δ) and specific structural characteristics, and that among non-Ortho-I superstructures, Ortho-II was reported as the only one exhibiting long-range interaction.
entities.evidence_span:
Detailed studies of these superstructures have primarily relied on highly sophisti-
cated experimental techniques, such as high-energy X-Ray diffraction at synchrotron
facilities and neutron scattering, which provide direct access to Oxygen ordering
within the bulk.

evidence_spans:
Detailed studies of these superstructures have primarily relied on highly sophisti-
cated experimental techniques, such as high-energy X-Ray diffraction at synchrotron
facilities and neutron scattering, which provide direct access to Oxygen ordering
within the bulk.
In addition, measurements of neutron diffraction have shown that different superstructures exhibit not only different occupancies (δ) but also specific characteristics for each one.[9, 18]
Although all superstructures (out of Ortho-I) present a two dimensional interaction, the Ortho-II superstructure has been reported as the only one exhibiting long-range interaction.

entities.name: The authors reject the explanation that a residual fraction of the sample remains entirely tetragonal: this would require an improbably ordered distribution of
entities.description: The authors reject the explanation that a residual fraction of the sample remains entirely tetragonal: this would require an improbably ordered distribution of oxygen vacancies (especially implausible in powder samples), and even if such a small tetragonal fraction existed it would be too small to produce XRD peaks comparable to the orthorhombic phase or to explain the selective appearance of peaks.
entities.evidence_span: The possibility that the corresponding δ fraction of the material remains entirely in the Tetragonal phase would imply a probabilistically unlikely ordering, given theoretical predictions that Oxygen vacancies within Cu-O chains repel each other.[16] Moreover, considering the nature of samples (powder), that option is even harder to achieve.[15]

evidence_spans: The possibility that the corresponding δ fraction of the material remains entirely in the Tetragonal phase would imply a probabilistically unlikely ordering, given theoretical predictions that Oxygen vacancies within Cu-O chains repel each other.[16] Moreover, considering the nature of samples (powder), that option is even harder to achieve.[15]

Furthermore, even if such a δ fraction of material in the Tetragonal phase existed, it would not be sufficient to produce peaks in an X-Ray diffractogram of comparable magnitude to those coming from the Orthorhombic phase (> 95 % in mass, since the 7 at.% of the YBCO would have one Oxygen less per unit cell). Nor would it explain selective peak appearance.

entities.name: The paper hypothesizes that during low-temperature oxygenation (below about 400 °C), YBCO passes through the Ortho-II region of the phase diagram, where oxygen
entities.description: The paper hypothesizes that during low-temperature oxygenation (below about 400 °C), YBCO passes through the Ortho-II region of the phase diagram, where oxygen ordering in the Ortho-II superstructure progressively organizes the Cu-O chain oxygen/vacancy configuration and thereby influences or forces the final oxygen ordering in the fully oxygenated orthorhombic/Ortho-I state, leaving a persistent, detectable structural fingerprint even near δ ≈ 0; this mechanism is proposed to explain the diffraction differences between the two preparation conditions.
entities.evidence_span: Based on experimental results, this work proposes the influence of the Oxy- gen order present in the Ortho-II superstructure of YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO), on the final ordering of Oxygens in its Orthorhombic phase for δ ≈0.

evidence_spans: Based on experimental results, this work proposes the influence of the Oxy- gen order present in the Ortho-II superstructure of YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO), on the final ordering of Oxygens in its Orthorhombic phase for δ ≈0.

Furthermore, we propose that, for low values of TO (TO < 400 oC), the T-O transition proceeds through the region of the phase diagram where the Ortho-II superstructure is present, leading to progressive ordering of the Oxygen atoms within the material.
Finally, we suggest that this mechanism is responsible for the differences observed between the diffractograms obtained under both conditions.

Accordingly, we propose the existence of a structural fingerprint associated with passage through the Ortho-II superstructure, persisting in the Oxygen-saturated state of the material, well within the Ortho-I ordered regime.

we propose that the presence of the Ortho-II superstructure in the path to the final configuration of the Orthorhombic phase is imprinting a lasting signature that is detectable even with commercial equipment.

We propose that this imprint is the result of the Ortho-II superstructure forcing the configuration of Oxygen (vacancies) sites in the Cu-O chains at the final configuration of the material after annealing.
We propose that passage through the Ortho-II superstructure during low-temperature oxygenation leaves a fingerprint that persists even at high oxygenation levels (δ ≈0).

entities.description: XRD shows the characteristic tetragonal-to-orthorhombic transition peak splitting around 2θ ≈ 47°: the tetragonal phase has one peak at 47°, while the orthorhombic phase has two peaks on either side; additionally, the 46° tetragonal peak disappears in all orthorhombic samples.
entities.evidence_span: The results show the typical peak splitting around the 2θ = 47o position upon transition from the Tetragonal to the Orthorhombic phase, where one peak is present at 47o for the Tetragonal phase and two peaks are present at both sides of 47o for the Orthorhombic one.[15]

evidence_spans: The results show the typical peak splitting around the 2θ = 47o position upon transition from the Tetragonal to the Orthorhombic phase, where one peak is present at 47o for the Tetragonal phase and two peaks are present at both sides of 47o for the Orthorhombic one.[15]
In addition, the peak at 46o associated with the Tetragonal phase disappears for all the experiments performed on the material in the Orthorhombic phase.

entities.name: The orthorhombic diffraction pattern depends on oxygenation temperature: for TO < 400 °C, the 47° peak splits but the original tetragonal peak remains present,
entities.description: The orthorhombic diffraction pattern depends on oxygenation temperature: for TO < 400 °C, the 47° peak splits but the original tetragonal peak remains present, whereas for TO > 400 °C, the 47° peak vanishes and is replaced by the two orthorhombic peaks.
entities.evidence_span: In particular, for low oxygenation temperatures (< 400 oC), the splitting of the 47o peak occurs, giving rise to two new peaks on both sides. However, the peak does not disappear; rather, it is still present.

evidence_spans: In particular, for low oxygenation temperatures (< 400 oC), the splitting of the 47o peak occurs, giving rise to two new peaks on both sides. However, the peak does not disappear; rather, it is still present.
On the other hand, at higher temperatures (> 400 oC), the 47o peak vanishes and it is replaced by the two peaks that characterize the Orthorhombic phase at both sides of the vanished one.

entities.name: The authors reject the explanation that a residual fraction of the sample remains entirely tetragonal: this would require an improbably ordered distribution of oxygen vacancies (especially implausible
entities.description: The authors reject the explanation that a residual fraction of the sample remains entirely tetragonal: this would require an improbably ordered distribution of oxygen vacancies (especially implausible in powder samples), and even if such a small tetragonal fraction existed it would be too small to produce XRD peaks comparable to the orthorhombic phase or to explain the selective appearance of peaks.
entities.evidence_span: The possibility that the corresponding δ fraction of the material remains entirely in the Tetragonal phase would imply a probabilistically unlikely ordering, given theoretical predictions that Oxygen vacancies within Cu-O chains repel each other.[16] Moreover, considering the nature of samples (powder), that option is even harder to achieve.[15]

entities.evidence_span: In addition, if this behavior were intrinsic to the Orthorhombic phase, diffraction patterns for both Orthorhombic cases should be similar in peak positions and relative intensities.[15]

entities.description: Passing through the Ortho-II region at low temperature during the tetragonal-to-orthorhombic transition leads to progressive oxygen ordering, and this ordering leaves a persistent structural fingerprint in the final YBCO configuration even beyond the Ortho-II stability region; the authors suggest this mechanism explains the differences between the diffractograms obtained under the two conditions.
entities.evidence_span: for low values of TO (TO < 400 oC), the T-O transition proceeds through the region of the phase diagram where the Ortho-II superstructure is present, leading to progressive ordering of the Oxygen atoms within the material.

entities.evidence_span: This conjecture is highly relevant, as it opens the pos-sibility of controlling the Ortho-I structural state in YBCO, enabling the design of superconducting materials with tunable anisotropic, electronic, and dynamical prop-erties.
